group.passage: At memory competitions, people race to memorize long lists of words, numbers or playing cards. Most of them rely on a technique known as the memory palace. Below, a memory champion explains how she uses it, and a brain scientist describes what research has revealed about it.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: A Walk Through My Grandmother’s House
passage_parts.text: People assume I was simply born this way, but at school I was the girl who forgot her homework at least once a week. What changed everything was a technique that is more than two thousand years old. According to legend, a Greek poet named Simonides once stepped out of a banquet just before the roof fell in, and he was able to name the victims by recalling where each guest had been sitting. Like him, I let places do the remembering. Before a contest, I take an imaginary walk through my grandmother’s house and drop one item at each stop along the way. To remember the word “violin”, for instance, I might picture one floating in her bathtub; the stranger the image, the better it sticks. Later, I simply repeat the walk in my mind and collect the items in order. Little by little, I went from losing track of a shopping list to recalling hundreds of digits.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Why the Method Works
passage_parts.text: Memory champions are not as different from the rest of us as we might think. When researchers scanned top memory athletes and compared them with other volunteers, they found no obvious differences in how their brains were built. What set the champions apart was activity: while memorizing, they relied heavily on areas that help us find our way around. In other words, the technique borrows our natural talent for remembering places. Better still, it can be learned. In one study, people who practiced the method every day for six weeks could recall almost as many words as the champions, and four months later they were still performing well. Their brain networks had even come to resemble those of the experts. Still, I would add a word of caution. The memory palace is excellent for lists, but storing a fact is not the same as understanding it, and it will not stop you from forgetting where you left your keys.

option_notes_zh.B: 大方向（這個方法有助於記憶）看似成立，但 Text B 最後明說記住一個事實不等於理解它；Text A 也只談記清單、數字，沒有說能幫助理解困難的概念。

4.explanation_zh: find one’s way around 表示「認得路、找到方向」，就是題幹 navigation（辨認方向、找路）的日常說法。Text B 說冠軍在記憶時大量使用腦中幫助我們「認路」的區域，所以這個技巧等於借用了我們記住地點的天賦。答案照文中寫 find our way around（只寫 find our way 也可以）。

translation_zh.text:
在記憶比賽中，參賽者比賽誰能更快記住一長串單字、數字或撲克牌。他們大多依靠一種叫做「記憶宮殿」的技巧。下面，一位記憶冠軍說明她怎麼運用它，一位腦科學家則介紹研究對它有哪些發現。

A　走過外婆的家
大家都以為我天生就是這樣，但在學校時，我是那個每週至少忘記帶一次作業的女生。改變一切的，是一種已有兩千多年歷史的技巧。根據傳說，一位名叫西摩尼得斯的希臘詩人有一次在屋頂坍塌之前剛好走出宴會，他憑著回想每位賓客坐在哪裡，說出了罹難者的名字。我也像他一樣，讓地點替我記憶。比賽前，我會在想像中走過外婆的家，沿途每一站放下一樣東西。例如要記住「小提琴」這個字，我可能會想像一把小提琴漂在她的浴缸裡；影像越奇怪，就記得越牢。之後，我只要在腦中重走一遍同樣的路線，依序把東西撿回來。一點一點地，我從記不住一張購物清單，進步到能記住上百個數字。

B　這個方法為什麼有效
記憶冠軍和我們其他人的差別，並不像我們以為的那麼大。研究人員掃描頂尖記憶選手的腦部，並和其他志願者比較時，發現他們的大腦在構造上沒有明顯的差異。讓冠軍與眾不同的是腦部的活動：記憶時，他們大量倚重幫助我們認路的區域。換句話說，這個技巧借用了我們天生記住地點的本領。更好的是，它是學得會的。在一項研究中，每天練習這個方法、持續六週的人，能記住的字幾乎和冠軍一樣多，四個月後表現依然很好。他們的腦部網絡甚至變得和專家的很像。不過，我要提醒一句。記憶宮殿很適合用來記清單，但記住一個事實和理解它並不相同，它也不能讓你不再忘記鑰匙放在哪裡。
